teacherGuide.overview: Uses torch batteries and electric fish to teach cells in series, voltage, current, complete circuits, and electrical safety.
learningGoals: Explain what voltage and current are and name their units.
State that a current needs a complete circuit.
Calculate the total voltage of cells in series.
Give three rules for staying safe near mains electricity.

beforeReading: Open a torch in front of the class. Ask: why are the batteries placed end to end and not side by side?
whileReading: After Page 2, groups light a bulb with one cell, then two, then three, and describe the brightness.
afterReading: Learners draw a circuit with three cells, a switch, and a bulb, and mark the total voltage.
discussion: Volta got his idea by studying a fish. What other inventions copy living things?
reflection: Which of the safety rules is broken most often where you live?

mathsExtension.task: How many 1.5-volt cells in series would you need to match the 860 volts of the strongest electric eel?
An eel has 6,000 cells, each giving 0.15 volts. What is the greatest voltage it could produce?

support: Let learners line up as “cells”, each holding a 1.5 card, and add the cards aloud.
stretch: Find out the difference between cells joined in series and cells joined in parallel.

factCheck.claim: 860-volt electric eel record (Brazil, 2019), ~0.15 V per electrocyte, West African electric catfish, Volta’s 1800 voltaic pile, and River Volta etymology.
factCheck.explanation: The 860-volt record (Electrophorus voltai, measured in Brazil, reported 2019) checked in November 2026. Each cell (~0.15 V), Malapterurus electricus in the Volta system, Volta’s 1800 pile, and the Portuguese origin of River Volta are standard references.
factCheck.reference: de Santana et al. (2019) Nature Communications / NaCCA Integrated Science curriculum (codes to verify)
